item.title: Semantic Edge-Cloud Communication for Real-Time Urban Traffic Digital Twins
item.description: arXiv:2610.14187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban traffic systems are becoming increasingly complex, demanding real-time traffic perception, proactive collision prediction, and intelligent management to improve safety and reduce congestion. Although AI-driven traffic management has shown strong promise, its success relies on diverse, high-quality data spanning critical scenarios such as collisions, near-collisions, and traffic rule violations. Digital twins offer a powerful solution by enabling synchronized virtual replicas of physical traffic environments for real-time monitoring, collision prediction, traffic-flow optimization, and diverse realistic scenario generation. However, continuously synchronizing a high-fidelity urban traffic digital twin through edge surveillance cameras requires substantial edge-cloud communication, and transmitting raw video streams leads to severe bandwidth and latency constraints. To overcome this challenge, this paper proposes a semantic communication-based edge-cloud framework for real-time urban traffic digital twin applications. By leveraging edge intelligence to extract and transmit only task-relevant semantic traffic information instead of full video feeds, the proposed framework significantly reduces communication overhead while preserving the essential dynamics needed for accurate real-time digital twin reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate more than 99% transmission savings and an average trajectory reconstruction error of only 0.12 m, confirming the proposed framework as an effective, scalable, and low-latency solution for AI-enabled urban traffic digital twin applications.
item.dc:creator: Murat Arda Onsu, Arman Dogru, Poonam Lohan, Burak Kantarci, Aisha Syed

item.title: An Availability Management Framework for Microservice-Based Safety-Critical CIoT Systems: Architecture and End-to-End Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety-critical Cellular Internet of Things (CIoT) systems increasingly rely on microservice architectures orchestrated across heterogeneous edge and cloud platforms. Although this paradigm improves modularity and scalability, the fault-tolerance mechanisms of contemporary orchestration platforms remain predominantly reactive, i.e., failed components are restarted or rescheduled only after an outage has already occurred. Such recovery can produce multi-second End to End Service Outage Time (E2E SOT), which can grow further under container restart backoff. This paper proposes an Availability Management Framework (AMF), a generic monitor-predict-recover loop that complements reactive recovery with machine learning-based anomaly detection and make-before-break switchover to a standby replica. Candidate ML models are evaluated offline under three protocols, including a change of operating regime, in order to select a model for live deployment. AMF is instantiated and evaluated on a three-tier tele-operated driving (ToD) testbed under a staged resource-exhaustion scenario. Relative to Kubernetes-only recovery, AMF completes switchover during the anomaly window, reduces E2E SOT, and avoids the tens-of-seconds outages associated with repeated in-place restarts under backoff. On this non-real-time testbed, residual E2E SOT lies inside healthy-path jitter and is therefore limited by path timing rather than by lateness of the recovery decision. The paper whows that coupling a validated ML based anomaly detector with proactive switchover can remove restart- and backoff-dominated outage from a critical path.
item.dc:creator: Hassaan Siddiqui, Ferhat Khendek

item.title: Harvesting-Aware Routing for Low-Latency Reliable Transmission in Interference-Powered Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.14250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a multi-hop wireless network where energy-harvesting nodes rely solely on ambient radio-frequency interference as their power source. The goal is to deliver a packet from source to destination with minimum latency while guaranteeing a target end-to-end outage probability under Rayleigh fading. This gives rise to a joint routing and power allocation problem in which interference plays a dual role: it provides harvestable energy, but also impairs link reliability. We first transform the intricate, multiplicative end-to-end outage constraint into an additive form. Then, we propose two optimal algorithms. The first, HOPE, minimizes the bottleneck harvesting latency, i.e., the longest energy-accumulation time along the path, by reducing the problem to a least-cost path computation on a graph with interference-aware link weights. The second, THOPE, extends the objective to total end-to-end latency, adding the cumulative transmission delay, and likewise admits a closed-form least-cost path solution. Both algorithms are solved in polynomial time via Dijkstra's algorithm and yield explicit expressions for the optimal transmit powers. Extensive simulations reveal that HOPE and THOPE reduce the average total latency by up to an order of magnitude compared with shortest-path and minimum-energy benchmarks, while exhibiting sharply concentrated delay distributions that are largely insensitive to interferer density.
item.dc:creator: Azadeh Sheikholeslami, Allan Nguyen

item.title: RADIUS-Assisted Companion PSK Discovery: Enabling WPA3-SAE in Externally Authenticated Multi-PSK (ePSK / MPSK / DPSK / iPSK / PPSK) Deployments
item.description: arXiv:2610.14410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large multi-dwelling unit (MDU), student-housing and hospitality networks rarely store resident pre-shared keys (PSKs) on the access point (AP). Instead, the per-resident keys of ePSK, MPSK, DPSK, iPSK or PPSK services are held in an external RADIUS server or cloud database synchronised with the property-management system. Our earlier work, Companion-BSSID-Assisted PSK Discovery (CAPD), brought WPA3-SAE to multi-PSK networks by learning the client's PSK on a WPA2-only companion BSSID and steering the client with IEEE 802.11v to a hidden WPA2/WPA3 primary BSSID of the same SSID. CAPD assumes that the AP can test every PSK itself. This paper removes that assumption. We propose RADIUS-Assisted Companion PSK Discovery (RA-CAPD). The AP forwards the ANonce, the raw EAPOL-Key message 2 (SNonce, MIC, RSNE), the SSID, the client MAC, the BSSID and the AP MAC to the external server in RADIUS vendor-specific attributes (VSAs). The server validates the MIC against all provisioned keys, identifies the matching PSK, and returns it encrypted under the RADIUS shared secret (or a per-AP key for cloud databases), together with the unit, room or user identity and the VLAN. The AP binds the client to this PSK and identity, synchronises the binding across all APs in the domain, and moves the client to the configured profile: 802.11v-capable clients via a BSS Transition Management request, and other clients by disconnection and reconnection. On that profile, SAE-capable clients complete WPA3-SAE and WPA2-only clients complete WPA2-PSK, both with the learned key and no further search, so the companion BSSID serves only for onboarding. We present the design, attribute dictionary, algorithms, complexity and security properties, together with laboratory validation on commercial access points.
item.dc:creator: Azif Abdul Salam Kolisam Beevi, Anil Kumar Reddy, Niraj Lochan Mahapatra

item.title: Energy-Aware Agentic Orchestration for Multi-Site Service Deployment
item.description: arXiv:2610.14793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy-aware orchestration across geographically distributed infrastructures is increasingly important as data centers absorb growing Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads. However, existing approaches often exclude the energy cost of automated decision-making from system-level sustainability assessments. This paper presents an energy-aware agentic orchestration framework that treats Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning as a measurable component of the control loop. We compare single-shot tool calling, ReAct, and plan-and-execute strategies on a multi-site Kubernetes testbed spanning two European data centers and instrumented at layers ranging from power distribution units to per-pod energy attribution. Using ten natural-language orchestration intents with varying decision complexity, we show that reasoning strategy and intent complexity strongly influence graphics processing unit (GPU) energy consumption during orchestration decisions. ReAct and plan-and-execute generated executable tool calls across all evaluated intents but required multiple LLM inferences, whereas the single-shot configuration was less costly but non-actionable. Prefix caching reduced mean ReAct GPU energy consumption by 29.4%. For the evaluated lightweight workload, the infrastructure-energy changes observed within the one-second measurement window were insufficient to offset the measured GPU decision energy. These findings demonstrate the importance of accounting for reasoning overhead when assessing the sustainability of AI-native orchestration and motivate energy-budgeted selection of agent strategies.

item.title: Stackelberg Game with Multi-Agent Transformer for ISRS-Aware Resource Re-optimization in Multi-Band Optical Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.14830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid expansion of generative AI is driving computing infrastructures toward interconnected AI data centers. Multi-band optical networks have become the backbone of such connectivity. To accommodate increasingly dynamic traffic demands, these networks require continual resource re-optimization to improve resource utilization and reduce service blocking. However, multi-band transmission amplifies inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering(ISRS), inducing nonlinear coupling among services. This coupling complicates re-optimization, as local adjustments perturb the global power profile, creating interdependent optimization decisions across services. Moreover, the nonlinear interactions vary with the subset of services selected for re-optimization, and inappropriate selection may reduce re-optimization effectiveness or diminish achievable benefits. To address these challenges, we propose a Stackelberg Game with Multi-Agent Transformer (SG-MAT) approach for ISRS-aware resource re-optimization. SG-MAT employs a leader-follower structure, in which the MAT-based follower models nonlinear coupling and generates coordinated channel reallocations, feeding the utilization improvements to the leader. Using this feedback, the leader identifies critical service subsets, approximating a Stackelberg equilibrium to guide global decisions and enabling consistent and efficient re-optimization. Simulation results show that SG-MAT achieves the highest utilization improvement and reduces the blocking ratio by approximately 30% under moderate traffic loads, with computational complexity comparable to benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxin Liu, Rentao Gu, Miao Zhu, Zeguang Zou, Hui Li, Yuefeng Ji

item.title: Conflict-Aware Autonomous Resource Orchestration for 5G Edge Slicing Using Multi-Agent Systems and LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 5G edge network slicing must reconcile two coupled requirements: understanding high-level operator intent and reallocating scarce computing and bandwidth resources under dynamic contention. Centralized optimization can face computational and responsiveness challenges under rapidly changing edge contention, and Multi-Agent System (MAS)-based auctions can support resource arbitration but still depend on operator-defined economic parameters and priorities. Embedding a Large Language Model (LLM) directly in a recurring control loop, by contrast, may introduce non-negligible inference latency and non-deterministic behavior. This paper proposes a two-timescale architecture that addresses this gap: an LLM-based Strategist translates natural-language network intents into economic policy parameters (budget, income, and bidding-aggressiveness) at the macro scale, while a deterministic, Vickrey-inspired second-price mechanism run by SPADE-based slice agents resolves recurring resource contention at the operational scale, with the resulting allocations enforced by patching Kubernetes CPU limits and Calico CNI bandwidth annotations directly on User Plane Function pods. We evaluate the architecture end-to-end on a real Kubernetes/Open5GS edge cluster across two complementary scenarios, each repeated 30 times: a Smart-City scenario, in which natural-language public-safety intents propagate into measurable changes in slice bids and bandwidth allocations within a few auction rounds, and a Hierarchical-slicing scenario, in which the mechanism provides priority-dependent resource and QoE differentiation, adapts to abrupt demand changes, and preserves configured minimum guarantees while maintaining near-complete allocation of the shared bandwidth pool.
item.dc:creator: Nathan R. Prediger, Rodrigo Moreira, Juliano Araujo Wickboldt, Tereza C. Carvalho, Pedro Oliveira, Paulo Novais, Fl\'avio de Oliveira Silva

item.title: Clock-Free Stochastic Scheduling for Real-Time Synchronized Content Delivery
item.description: arXiv:2610.15114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time synchronized content delivery is critical for applications such as cloud gaming, collaborative mixed reality, and live streaming, where a server must ensure that a group of users perceives the same content simultaneously for each delivery. Due to heterogeneous and unpredictable network delays, ensuring synchronization is highly challenging. We propose a clock-free scheduling framework that introduces latency compensation to control the server's delivery time for each user, aiming to maximize synchronization performance (i.e., minimizing the gap between the maximum and minimum latencies) while maintaining a low overall latency cost. Unlike prior work requiring synchronized clocks or client-side timestamps, our approach uses only acknowledgment feedback, enabling flexible deployment across diverse environments. We formulate the problem as a convex stochastic optimization with a non-smooth objective. To solve the problem, we employ the stochastic proximal point (SPP) algorithm that updates the delay compensation, using only the previous latency samples, rather than the latency distribution. By exploiting the subproblem structure, we apply ADMM to enable efficient updates with per-iteration complexity of at most $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$, where $N$ is the number of users. We establish a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$, where $K$ is the number of content deliveries for transmission. The framework is further extended to handle transmission failures, where packet loss results in successful delivery to only a subset of users. Finally, simulations using both synthetic and real-world latency traces demonstrate the consistent superiority of our algorithm against baseline methods.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Wang, Xiaoyi Wu, Ying Sun, Atilla Eryilmaz, Bin Li

item.title: Tutorial on Closed-Loop and Application-Aware Digital Twins for Future Wireless Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.15120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To support emerging applications such as extended reality, autonomous systems, and large-scale cyber-physical infrastructures, next-generation wireless networks must evolve beyond traditional communication paradigms toward tightly integrated and closed-loop systems. Digital Twin Networks (DTNs) have recently emerged as a key enabler of this transformation by bridging the physical and digital worlds through real-time, bidirectional interactions and adaptive control mechanisms. In this tutorial, we provide a comprehensive overview of DTN design and optimization across multiple system dimensions. Specifically, we first introduce the fundamental design principles of DTN creation, including high-fidelity twin modeling, telemetry integration, and cyber-physical synchronization. We then present resource optimization and semantic-driven DTNs, where application-aware objectives and semantic abstractions guide efficient data processing, communication, and decision-making. Subsequently, we explore physical-layer optimization techniques for DTNs, emphasizing joint sensing, communication, and adaptive wireless resource control. Furthermore, we examine DTN-guided network management and feedback optimization, focusing on closed-loop learning, real-time control, and reinforcement-driven adaptation between digital twins and physical networks. Finally, we review ongoing standardization efforts and enabling tools that support the practical deployment of DTNs in real-world systems. This tutorial aims to provide a unified perspective on DTNs as an emerging paradigm for application-aware, AI-native, and closed-loop wireless systems, and to highlight key challenges and future research directions in this rapidly evolving field.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Liu, Sara Garcia Sanchez, Mingzhe Chen, Xingqin Lin, Berk Canberk, Tommaso Melodia

item.title: NAS Timers for Non-Terrestrial Networks: Current Standards and Directions
item.description: arXiv:2610.15211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Response-supervision timers in the 5G Non-Access Stratum (NAS) bound the time allowed for signaling exchanges before retransmission or abnormal-case handling begins. In non-terrestrial networks, that interval can include satellite propagation, terrestrial transport, and processing by multiple core-network functions. Under current 3GPP specifications, the applicable timer value for satellite access is selected according to the satellite NG-RAN radio access technology (RAT) type. However, control paths within the same low Earth orbit (LEO) network can differ in propagation delay and processing load. This article reviews the relevant 3GPP timer semantics and traces the delay components covered by different timers through 5G registration. It organizes candidate refinements along two dimensions: configuration granularity and information scope. A registration case study illustrates the trade-off between avoiding premature timer expiry and recovering promptly from message loss. The article identifies the information and coordination that future specifications would need to address to support interoperable timer configuration.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Liu, Peng Hu

item.title: Cost-Aware Conflict Triage for xApp Control Conflicts in Open RAN
item.description: arXiv:2610.15310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) enables multi-vendor deployments where concurrent RAN control applications (xApps) independently optimise mobility, load, coverage, and energy within the Near Real Time RAN Intelligent Controller (Near-RT RIC). When xApps act on overlapping control parameters, their isolated loops produce conflicting decisions that degrade the network Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Existing conflict-evaluation methods estimate severity but do not answer whether the intervention is cost-justified. This paper proposes a cost-aware conflict triage framework that pairs ECDF-based severity evaluation with an event-level decision layer. The framework groups detected conflict records into episodes, extracts nine features, estimates per-mechanism costs and benefits, and assigns one of three actions: tolerate, defer, or mitigate. Evaluated in a simulator-driven Open RAN setting over 30 Monte Carlo runs with four concurrent xApps, the framework defers 66.8 %, mitigates 19.8 %, and tolerates 13.4 % of detected episodes, achieving a mean net utility of 0.132 per intervention, 3.9x higher than an always-mitigate baseline, by avoiding low- value interventions through cost-aware selectivity.
item.dc:creator: Abdul Wadud, Fatemeh Golpayegani, Nima Afraz

item.title: The Evolution of In-Premise Networks In the Era of Immersive Services: From Copper to Fiber-to-The Room [Invited Tutorial]
item.description: arXiv:2610.15566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The telecommunications industry is shifting toward an experience-driven era defined by immersive applications that impose stringent network demands. While passive optical network (PON)-based Fiber-To-The-Home (FTTH) architectures have historically delivered high-capacity broadband, a growing performance gap between access and indoor networks necessitates driving fiber deeper into premises. Complementing existing copper and WiFi technologies, Fiber-to-the-Room (FTTR) is emerging as a critical enabler. This article examines the drivers of this architectural shift, specifically focusing on collaborative extended reality (XR). We analyze the multi-modal traffic characteristics and Quality-of-Experience (QoE) requirements of XR, alongside the resulting network performance implications. To address these demands, we propose a novel resource allocation framework integrating coarse-grained traffic forecasting with intelligent in-premise roaming. This framework facilitates the flexible deployment of artificial intelligence models tailored to the computational capabilities of the FTTH, FTTR, and WiFi segments. Numerical evaluations of a representative multi-tier network demonstrate that long-horizon, multi-step-ahead traffic forecasts significantly reduce inference frequency. This approach enables coordinated resource allocation and network-orchestrated seamless mobility across rooms, effectively satisfying collaborative XR QoE requirements. Finally, we highlight strategies to amortize FTTR capital expenditure by extending the optical infrastructure's role beyond basic connectivity. By supporting diverse services over a unified physical layer, FTTR enhances infrastructure utilization, unlocks novel revenue streams, and maximizes the value of in-premise fiber deployments.
item.dc:creator: Elaine Wong, Sourav Mondal

item.title: Coarse-Grained Predictive Resource Allocation Framework enabling In-Premise XR Collaborations
item.description: arXiv:2610.15581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Immersive extended reality (XR) applications are key enablers of human-centric connectivity in next-generation networks. However, meeting their high-throughput, ultra-low-latency, and high-reliability demands while preventing cyber-sickness remains a critical challenge, especially in environments with non-deterministic wireless connectivity. Fiber-To-The-Room (FTTR), extending widely deployed Fiber-To-The-Home (FTTH) infrastructure, offers a promising solution. Yet, satisfying the stringent Quality-of-Experience (QoE) requirements of XR collaborators demands robust resource allocation across the multi-tier cascade of FTTH, FTTR, and WiFi segments. In this paper, we propose a coarse-grained traffic forecasting-empowered proactive resource allocation and intelligent in-premise roaming framework. Here, artificial intelligence (AI) model complexities are scaled to the computational capabilities of each network segment. At the FTTR segment, we employ a hybrid temporal convolutional and bi-directional long short-term memory (TCN-BiLSTM) network for multi-modal XR traffic forecasting, integrating passive optical network (PON) and WiFi access points with multi-link operation (MLO) and orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA). The resulting long-horizon forecasts reduce inference frequency, enabling coordinated FTTR-WiFi resource allocation and seamless network-orchestrated mobility across rooms. At the FTTH segment, we deploy Transformer-based time-series models (e.g., Informer, Autoformer, PatchTST, and TFT) to predict the complex XR traffic aggregated in FTTR segments for transmission over the FTTH backhaul. Evaluations show Transformer-based models are up to $\sim$75% more accurate in long-horizon forecasting than the hybrid model. Extensive simulations confirm the proposed framework significantly outperforms traditional methods in satisfying XR QoE requirements.
item.dc:creator: Sourav Mondal, Elaine Wong

item.title: NetRL: Powering Network Decisions via NetGRPO-Driven Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.16226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network decision-making tasks, including adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control, require policies to process heterogeneous states and actions while balancing near- and long-term consequences. Existing solutions generalize poorly across network tasks, require substantial task-specific redesign, and lack reliable evaluation of long- horizon action consequences. Methods that learn through online interaction additionally face unstable optimization. We present NetRL, a two-stage LLM-based reinforcement learning framework that combines supervised fine-tuning on demonstration trajectories with online policy optimization. A universal mixed-embedding interface combines textual task descriptions with precise numerical states, while a network action head produces valid decisions. At its core, NetGRPO evaluates candidate actions over multiple future trajectories, directs deeper search toward uncertain alternatives through confidence-aware budgeting, and performs group-relative, clipped, and KL-regularized updates. NetRL achieves 23.6% higher QoE than NetLLM, 12.2% lower job completion time than Genet, and 24.1% higher network utility than Orca, yielding state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods. Confidence-aware budgeting reduces end-to-end training time by 27.1% without reducing validation QoE. NetRL also converges stably and generalizes to unseen network traces without retraining. Code and model weights are available at the repository linked in this paper.
item.dc:creator: Lingfeng Peng, Xiaohui Xie, Yang Bao, Yong Cui

item.title: Island-Ready Communication Networks: Connectivity Monitoring and State Synchronization for 5G Crisis Connectivity at the Edge
item.description: arXiv:2610.16284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Island-ready 5G deployments provide edge connectivity for isolated regions in crisis scenarios by switching to island operation when they are cut off from the global Internet. This work addresses open research challenges that hinder the practical realization of island readiness, with a focus on the required state synchronization and connectivity monitoring functionality. As a proof of concept and for performance evaluation, we integrate our solutions in open-source projects and emulate a country-wide 5G communication network with real-world cellular traffic. Our evaluation studies the switching latency of transitions to island operation, showing that most of the transition delay stems from the access network reconfiguration. We study the synchronization overhead of a highly distributed core network, finding that the synchronization traffic grows faster than linearly with the number of 5G cores, reaching peak synchronization data rates of 9.36MB/s for a deployment of 50 cores.
item.dc:creator: Leon Janzen, Maria Koch, Matthias Hollick

item.title: CALIPER: Calibrating HPC/AI Network Simulators
item.description: arXiv:2610.16477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network simulation plays an important role in HPC/AI system research by enabling exploration of network architectures, communication strategies, and system configurations at scales that may be impractical to study experimentally. Existing approaches to network simulator calibration and validation lack a principled methodology that combines parameter alignment, constrained inference, and independent validation for collective-centric HPC/AI networks. We present CALIPER, a methodology for systematic calibration and validation of HPC/AI network simulators. CALIPER distinguishes directly observable system parameters from auxiliary parameters which are configured via calibration and constrains the latter to feasible domains consistent with the target system. We evaluate CALIPER's hierarchical, scale-aware calibration and its effects on parameter identifiability and generalization using collective communication benchmarks on a reference system with up to 64-nodes at the J\"ulich Supercomputing Centre. Validation results show that the calibrated parameter configurations identified by CALIPER predict system performance with less than 5% mean errors across scale-up and scale-out network domains. CALIPER demonstrates that hierarchical, constrained calibration can produce simulator configurations whose predictive accuracy persists beyond the observations used for fitting.
item.dc:creator: Seyyidahmed Lahmer, Daniel Seibel, Srijeet Basu, Arno Troch, Jayesh Badwaik, Subhomoy Bhattacharyya, Abubakr Nada, Debjyoti Bhattacharjee, Vinay Kumar Baapanapalli Yadaiah, Michael Peeters, Andreas Herten, Darayus Adil Patel

item.title: Offline-Tuned Service-Aware TN-NTN Feeder Allocation for 6G Post-Disaster Service Resilience
item.description: arXiv:2610.16501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terrestrial network (TN) failures during disasters can overload surviving base stations (BSs) and disrupt emergency services. A non-terrestrial network (NTN) provides fallback, but its feeder link can become a bottleneck as users migrate. This paper studies post-disaster network resilience through service-priority-aware orchestration of constrained NTN feeder capacity in a post-failure snapshot. A lightweight Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) tunes feeder, offload, and user-ranking parameters offline, not as an online artificial intelligence (AI) controller. A Python system-level simulator sweeps operating regions under abstract TN-NTN link and queueing models. Gains depend on failure severity. At a 180-Mbps feeder under total TN outage, the proposed policy increases the absolute emergency-weighted continuity metric Cemg from 0.399 to 0.666 relative to the matched rule baseline with uniform feeder scaling (paired gain: 0.267; 95% bootstrap CI: [0.264, 0.271]); mild damage can reduce aggregate continuity. Offline CEM feeder-weight tuning further improves severe-failure continuity over fixed service priorities, whereas tuned offload and user ranking provide no detectable incremental gain.
item.dc:creator: Donglin Wang, Anjie Qiu, Qiuheng Zhou, Hans D. Schotten

item.title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
item.description: arXiv:2610.17091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.
item.dc:creator: Michele Ferrero, Gabriele Castellano, Paolo Medagliani, Sebastien Martin, Roberto Morabito, Massimo Gallo

item.title: Computing All-Pairs Shortest Communication Time Paths for Periodically Varying Satellite Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.17372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We address the problem of designing an efficient algorithm for computing the all-pairs shortest-time paths in time-varying networks, specifically targeting the dynamic topological characteristics of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. We model such temporal graphs as $G = (V, E_t)$, where $V=\{1, 2,\ldots , n\}$ is the set of $n$ vertices in the graph, and $E_t$ is the set of $M$ time-varying edges considered over a total time window of size $T = M\tau$, $\tau$ being the duration of each interval in that time window. For such a network, our algorithm finds the all-pair shortest paths in $O(M^2n^3)$-time. A key advantage of our approach is its computational structure, which mirrors two matrix multiplication steps, first in the forward direction and then in the backward direction. This structure of the algorithm makes it exceptionally suitable for parallelization on SIMD architectures like GPUs, thereby offering a significant speedup over traditional shortest-path algorithms and enabling efficient, network-wide message routing in rapidly changing LEO satellite constellations.
item.dc:creator: Koushik Sinha, Dibakar Saha, Sai Puppala, Bhabani P. Sinha

item.title: What Is the Cost of a Handover Interruption? Rethinking 5G Mobility for Aerial Vehicles
item.description: arXiv:2610.17380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-altitude aviation is moving toward large-scale operations increasingly dependent on 5G cellular connectivity. However, 5G mobility remains blind to the operational risk of its decisions: the same interruption may be harmless in cruise over an empty field but critical near obstacles, crowds or other aircraft. Although 5G already provides mechanisms to obtain location, population density, and radio conditions, mobility decisions do not translate this information into an operational risk metric. We propose Risk-Aware Mobility (RAM), which maps predicted communication disruptions to an operational-risk proxy using information staleness, position uncertainty, and operational context, and exposes this risk to existing mobility mechanisms. In a dense S\~ao Paulo deployment with 188 licensed 5G sectors, risk-aware handover timing reduces the mean operational-risk proxy by 45\% relative to conventional A3 without degrading serving-link quality. These results motivate shifting 5G mobility from optimizing handover performance to managing the operational risk of mobility decisions. Beyond handover timing, this perspective raises a broader question: which cells should serve aerial operations when connectivity is evaluated by operational risk rather than radio performance alone?
item.dc:creator: Andr\'e Melo, Yueqi Chen, Igor Kadota, Louren\c{c}o Alves Pereira Jr

item.title: QoE-Aware Service Function Chain Orchestration in Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks for In-Flight Internet
item.description: arXiv:2610.17851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In remote regions lacking terrestrial infrastructure, aviation users increasingly demand Internet services comparable to ground cellular networks. This paper proposes a space-air-ground integrated network (SAGIN) architecture that combines ground networks, civil aviation networks, and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Based on real North Atlantic flight data, a heterogeneous aviation Internet is constructed to support diverse aircraft service requirements. A composite Quality of Experience (QoE) metric, characterized by transmission delay, jitter, and content similarity, guides efficient resource utilization. The dynamic connectivity of SAGIN is modeled using a reconfigurable time-expanded graph (RTEG). With Network Function Virtualization (NFV), data delivery is formulated as a Service Function Chain (SFC) deployment across ground stations, relay aircraft, and satellites, resulting in a long-term QoE maximization problem. A tailored Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) algorithm incorporating LCSS-based path filtering and softmax-based action selection is developed. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach enables seamless connectivity for heterogeneous aircraft and consistently outperforms game-theoretic and MATD3 methods in terms of QoE.
item.dc:creator: Feng Liu, Bing Du, Ziyang Guo, Xiaoqi Zhang, Haijun Zhang

item.title: Towards Virtual Networking for a Time-Triggered Hypervisor
item.description: arXiv:2610.17899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtualization enables mixed-criticality applications to run on shared hardware by isolating them within separate virtual machines (VMs). However, achieving end-to-end timing guarantees for critical tasks hosted on virtual CPUs (VCPUs) without relying on static partitioning is hard. A possible solution is a time-triggered hypervisor that dispatches VMs' VCPUs to processor cores according to a predetermined global schedule. A global schedule includes the computation, the network, and the virtualization layer to provide end-to-end timing guarantees across hosts and VMs during design time. In this work, we propose a VirtIO-based virtual network that realizes IEEE 802.1Qbv quasi-compliant inter-VM communication, providing predictable timing for critical messages exchanged between time-triggered VMs. We present our VirtIO-based virtual network architecture and derive network-level scheduling constraints that emerge from the properties of the proposed solution. We implement the proposed design in the ACRN hypervisor and evaluate the end-to-end latency of critical traffic in a loaded network, demonstrating that our time-triggered VirtIO-net prototype provides predictable end-to-end latency under load.
item.dc:creator: Jan Ruh, Silviu S. Craciunas, Jan Korecky

item.title: Shortcut in Generalization: Rethinking Evaluation Protocol for Encrypted Traffic Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.17961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encrypted traffic classification is commonly evaluated under a range of experimental protocols, with classification performance reported as the primary measure. However, the reported performance may be influenced by shortcuts left uncontrolled in the evaluation protocol, such as shortcut features and cross-partition sharing, rather than reflect generalizable traffic patterns. And test-only feature transformations may further introduce train-test mismatch. In this paper, we study how current evaluation protocols are affected by shortcut-related factors, including field-level shortcuts, cross-partition sharing, and train-test processing. We compare feature importance, retrained feature removal, and field-only split sensitivity. We also vary Source-IP overlap and packets per flow, compare test-only IP transformations with matched train-test transformations. Experiments on three public datasets show that the performance of existing methods are affected by both cross-partition sharing and the consistency of train-test transformations. Specifically, increasing Source-IP overlap from 0% to 100% raises accuracy by about 32-33 points before identifier masking, compared with only about 8 points after masking. For two state-of-the-art pretrained models (i.e., YaTC and NetMamba), the 11-13 points loss caused by test-only IP zeroing is almost fully recovered when the same transformation is applied during both training and testing.
item.dc:creator: Qiming Yu, Chungang Lin, Zhengyi Ma, Zijia Song, Yuliang Lu, Guozheng Yang, Dongzhen Qi

item.title: CALM-5G: Event-Level Conformal Risk Control for Predictive Service-Assurance Alarms
item.description: arXiv:2610.17962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predictive service assurance converts forecasts of key performance indicators into alarms, and that conversion decides whether the assurance function is deployable. We present CALM-5G, an assurance layer that operates above any forecasting backbone and issues alarms with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. It calibrates on service-level violation events, scores violation onset directly, selects its calibration scheme out of sample, and reports the alarm duty cycle with every certified miss rate. Four corpora are evaluated separately, namely a production cellular network, commercial 5G traces, an open radio access network testbed and our 5G standalone testbed. Risk control on the regression-derived score yields duty cycles of 0.24 to 0.91. Onset targeting with cross-validated calibration reduces time-in-alarm by 56.3% to 89.7% on three corpora, with no significant change on the fourth. The realised miss rate stays within a two-standard-error tolerance on three corpora and within one standard error of it on the fourth. Under label shift, pooled batch calibration exceeds that tolerance structurally, by 10.9 standard errors on the production corpus. Online calibration restores compliance. Calibration schemes cannot be ranked on the split that fits their thresholds. Miss rate and duty cycle are certified jointly where within-entity dependence leaves sufficient calibration units.
item.dc:creator: \"{O}mer Faruk \.{I}\c{s}canl{\i}, Ya\u{g}mur Sabucu Sandal

item.title: NetCoFi: A Budget-Aware Coarse-Fine Dual-Branch Model for Encrypted Traffic Classification
item.description: arXiv:2610.17978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encrypted traffic classification is critical for network management and security, but practical deployment must balance classification accuracy and inference cost. Existing models typically process fixed flow windows with limited control over computation after training, which can limit the accuracy-efficiency trade-off under constrained resources. To address this problem, we present NetCoFi, a budget-aware classifier that allocates computation at coarse and fine granularities. Using byte representations and observable packet metadata, NetCoFi selects token neighborhoods for fine-grained encoding while compressing the full window into complementary coarse context. Multi-budget training enables the same model to operate at different routing budgets without retraining. Evaluation on six public datasets shows that NetCoFi achieves state-of-the-art classification performance when trained from scratch. Under low-budget settings, NetCoFi improves average Macro-F1 by 7.86 percentage points across three datasets, compared with a same-depth static baseline. In a DPDK-GPU traffic processing pipeline, it increases mean batch throughput from 26.42 to 43.42 Mb/s, a 1.64x improvement over NetMamba.
item.dc:creator: Zhengyi Ma, Qiming Yu, Chungang Lin, Wentao Cui, Zijia Song, Guozheng Yang

item.title: Developments in Building Towards the Indian SKA Regional Centre
item.description: arXiv:2610.18091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The SKA Regional Centre Network (SRCNet) is a federated global network designed to archive, distribute, and process SKAO data products. This paper examines the evolving SRCNet architecture-focusing on the transition to version 0.2 (v0.2) requirements, including computation, orchestration, and multi-tiered storage-and details the strategy for establishing its proto-SRC infrastructure. We outline the prototype developments for the major and minor nodes in the context of v0.2. We describe the minor node compute and storage demands, establishing a pathway toward a fully operational Indian SKA Regional Centre (INSRC).
item.dc:creator: Rohit Sharma (Department of Space, Planetary & Astronomical Sciences & Engineering), Yogesh Wadadekar (National Centre for Radio Astrophysics, Pune University Campus, Ganeshkhind, Pune, Maharashtra, India)

item.title: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
item.description: arXiv:2610.18406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time. In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift. We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Qingyang Li, Yunpeng Tan, Mingxin Yang, Yannan Hu, Lei Zhang, Yong Cui, Zongming Guo, Xinggong Zhang

item.title: An Optical KV Cache Network for Disaggregated LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2610.18444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disaggregated LLM serving moves each request's KV cache from a prefill GPU to a decode GPU before the response begins, and a coding-agent turn often moves the KV of its whole long context. Behind an oversubscribed packet fabric this transfer adds to time to first token (TTFT). An optical circuit switch (OCS) can give every transfer a full-rate circuit for less than an oversubscribed packet fabric costs, but a mechanical OCS needs tens of milliseconds to reconfigure. We hide this delay inside the prefill. A reservation scheduler commits each circuit while the prefill is still computing, so the circuit is ready when the KV is, and each GPU reaches the OCS over its own wavelength-multiplexed (WDM) optics on one fiber pair. In simulations of GPU clusters on real serving traces with measured prefill times on H100 GPUs, this optical KV cache network matches 400G packet fabrics with adaptive routing at 0.55 to 0.78 times the cost of a 2:1 fabric and tolerates the 50 ms reconfiguration delay of a 384-port mechanical OCS.
item.dc:creator: Seongwon Yoon, Shimeng Yu

item.title: Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction through LoRA Federated Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.18640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Intelligent Transport Systems, protecting vulnerable road users, specifically pedestrians, is a paramount challenge. The present work contributes to this field, putting forth a distributed architecture in which vehicles connected to the cellular infrastructure collect pedestrians' trajectories and fine-tune a foundation model for pedestrian trajectory forecasting via federated training. A server positioned at the edge of the cellular network is responsible for aggregating the local model's parameters from the vehicles and updating the global model's parameters. To reduce radio resource utilization, Low-Rank Adaptation is proposed; to decrease both the number and the size of updates, an increase in the number of training rounds performed by the vehicles per communication round is put forth. A novel figure of merit is then introduced to quantify the use of radio resources dedicated to Vehicle-to-Infrastructure communications as required by the federated solution. The proposed scheme delivers excellent prediction accuracy while significantly reducing the communication cost compared to alternative federated training methods. This shows that combining fine-tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation, and a reduction of the communication periodicity between the vehicles and the edge server is key to enabling a distributed approach to trajectory prediction in vehicular environments.
item.dc:creator: Simone Travagliati, Maria Luisa Merani

item.title: HILO: Enabling Low-power, Dual-Band Communication using Tunnel Diode Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2610.18641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wireless communication remains the most power-consuming operation in embedded systems. Low-power transmitters such as backscatter achieve microwatt-scale operation but produce weak signals susceptible to in-band interference and frequency-selective fading, particularly in non-line-of-sight settings. Multi-band transmission can mitigate these effects through spectral-domain redundancy rather than temporal-domain redundancy, improving reliability without sacrificing bitrate or latency. However, conventional multi-band radio transceivers require duplicated RF chains or power-hungry synthesizers. We introduce HILO, a tunnel diode-based frontend that enables dual-band operation from a single circuit. HILO inverts the conventional paradigm: rather than suppressing the harmonics inherent to tunnel diode nonlinearity, it harnesses them. An external device injection-locks the oscillator to a fundamental frequency, simultaneously stabilizing a higher harmonic and yielding two injection-locked carriers without a second oscillator or frequency multiplier. In transmit mode, HILO exploits self-oscillating mixing to modulate both carriers simultaneously; in receive mode, it uses autodyne downconversion at both frequencies. By turning an inherent nonlinearity into a feature, HILO achieves dual-band links while consuming under 210 $\mu$W.
item.dc:creator: Dhairya Shah, Rajashekar Reddy Chinthalapani, Pramuka Sooriya Patabandige, Ambuj Varshney

item.title: Ghostline: a six-node Wi-Fi CSI motion tracker with node-to-node Links. System description and a pilot evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.18764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ghostline is a device-free motion tracking system built on six ESP32-S3 Wi-Fi boards and one consumer router. The boards' Wi-Fi driver reports channel state information (CSI) for every received frame with the sender's address, and a modified open-source firmware forwards both, so every board carries a CSI stream for the router and for each other board: seven radios give up to 36 directed Links over 21 Spans instead of a star of six. Each Link is compared with a self-forming quiet Baseline, disturbed Links vote on a floor grid, and the grid becomes anonymous Tracks. The system was built and run during a three-day hackathon in an ordinary room. We describe it in full and report a pilot evaluation with one walker: spoken cues at seven marked positions, a two-minute free walk and five minutes of empty room, synchronised to video within 0.18 s (median). Walking between marks, the Track lay a median 0.85 m from the straight path and 1.56 m (95% CI 1.29 to 2.83) from a cue-based reference trajectory (constant speed between cues, not measured positions), with 46% of walk updates within 2 m of it; the free walk was tracked in 94% of updates. The limits: a standing person is lost within seconds, a false Track appeared in 15.9% and 2.9% of updates in two empty-room periods, and informal runs that afternoon did not separate two walkers. Two offline replays through the same pipeline show where this comes from: with the node-to-node Links removed and settings unchanged, the tracked share of walk updates falls from 90% to 19% and the free walk from 96% to 60%; a plain radio tomographic image on the same per-Span evidence, at the same false rate, matches the grid and tracker at 2 m (48% against 47%) and is ahead at 1 m (36% against 21%). On this recording the Tracks depend on the Link set, and the imaging stage adds no measurable accuracy. We state what the pilot establishes and what it does not.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Cochinescu, Ionut Moldovanu, Alexandru Constantin

item.title: Learning to Sync at the Edge: Client-Side Adaptive Synchronization for Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14268v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The scalability and performance of edge federated learning are fundamentally constrained by synchronization bottlenecks. Clients operate under heterogeneous compute, time-varying communication conditions, and, in some settings, privacy constraints, yet synchronization is often still handled with fixed schedules. However, synchronization decisions are often made outside the client, even though the client directly observes local progress, resource state, and communication conditions. We present a client-side reinforcement learning synchronization framework in which each client decides during training whether to upload, download, synchronize bidirectionally, or defer communication. The framework places a lightweight scheduler alongside the local model and formulates synchronization as a resource-aware control problem driven by local learning and system state. We study this framework on two representative edge workloads, spatiotemporal traffic forecasting and image classification. Across both settings, adaptive client-side synchronization improves the accuracy-cost trade-off, reducing system cost in traffic forecasting while maintaining competitive cost and improving final accuracy in image classification. We also consider privacy-constrained settings, where synchronization must account for not only latency and energy but also privacy expenditure. Overall, our results show that synchronization in edge federated learning is better treated as an adaptive client-side control problem than only as a server-side coordination mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Ebasa Temesgen, Ammar Ahmed, Nathan Lechamo, Ali Anwar, Maria Gini

item.title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
item.description: arXiv:2610.14483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.
item.dc:creator: Milind Srivastava, Zeying Zhu, Peilin Xin, Yancheng Yuan, Zaoxing Liu, Vyas Sekar

item.title: Declared but Unaccountable: Measuring the Seller-Identity Gap in Advertising Supply-Chain Transparency
item.description: arXiv:2610.14661v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public advertising transparency relies on a minimum accountability condition: an account authorized by a publisher in ads.txt or app-ads.txt should appear in the applicable sellers.json registry. When an available registry omits the declared seller ID, the authorization remains visible and machine-readable, but its public verification path breaks. We call this failure the seller-identity gap. We measure the gap using 233.4 million normalized advertising-transparency records and an absent-only, coverage-aware evidence rule. A declaration enters the numerator only when the applicable registry is available and omits its seller ID; unavailable, malformed, confidential, and other non-evaluable states remain separate. The resulting row-level floor is 24.25% in a high-popularity, low-removal reference population and 30.71% among publishers associated with at least 100 copyright-removal requests, a 6.45 percentage-point increase. The gap then remains near one third at stricter cumulative thresholds. Standardizing the populations to common weights over 1,469 shared ad systems reduces the primary contrast to 4.65 points: about 72% remains within systems, while 28% forms a composition-associated residual. We connect these population estimates to recurring seller-account coordinates, byte-identical declaration configurations, and provenance-bearing case packets. We frame this declaration-centered investigative use of public advertising records as Ad Transparency Intelligence: it reconstructs declared supply-chain relationships, identifies where public verification stops, and prioritizes evidence for corroboration without equating correlation with attribution. Advertising transparency supports accountability and investigation only when visible authorizations remain publicly verifiable.
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Grotto, Alessandro Cantelli-Forti, Alessio Merlo

item.title: CESNET-TimeSeries26: A Multi-Year Network Traffic Time Series Dataset for Annual Seasonality, Concept Drift, and Long-Term Anomaly Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.14799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Forecast-based models are fundamental to network traffic management and anomaly detection. However, it is essential to evaluate these forecasting models over extended periods of time in order to assess their adaptability to unexpected phenomena and shifts in underlying patterns. This kind of long-term evaluation requires multi-year data to account for yearly seasonality and behavioral drift. Existing public datasets are too short to support such long-horizon forecasting tasks. We introduce CESNET-TimeSeries26, comprising 995 days of continuous traffic time series from the CESNET3 network, together with a single subnet spanning approximately 4.5 years. The dataset captures 278,466 IP addresses, 285 institutions, and 566 institutional subnets at three aggregation intervals. The dataset provides a definitive longitudinal benchmark for evaluating forecasting models in both operational management and security monitoring. We demonstrate that annual seasonality is the dominant periodic component. Moreover, we show that a forecasting model can exploit the annual component only when its training window covers at least one complete annual cycle, which no sub-year dataset provides.
item.dc:creator: Josef Koumar, Karel Hynek, Kamil Jerabek, Pavel Siska

item.title: DualColl: Throughput-Optimal Bandwidth-Bound Collective Communications via Fractional Tree Packing
item.description: arXiv:2610.15704v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale distributed training increasingly makes collective communication bandwidth-bound. In modern GPU clusters, communication libraries such as NCCL implement collectives including AllReduce over heterogeneous interconnects such as NVLink, InfiniBand, and Ethernet, making efficient use of available network bandwidth a central systems challenge. ForestColl showed that collective communication on such fabrics can be formulated using fractional tree packing; its scalable polynomial-time construction is developed for AllGather, with AllReduce obtained by composing AllGather and ReduceScatter. We present DualColl, which targets bandwidth-bound AllReduce directly. Under the tree-based AllReduce model, DualColl applies a Garg--K\"onemann-style multiplicative-weights algorithm and, for any $0<\epsilon<1$, computes a feasible schedule whose throughput is at least $(1-\epsilon)^2$ of the optimal AllReduce throughput. Its key component is an exact minimum-cost collective-tree oracle that projects physical-link dual prices onto a logical graph of participating ranks, reducing each iteration to shortest-path computations followed by a minimum spanning tree. We further extend the framework to local equal-next-hop packet-sprayed routing and to networks without explicit per-tree bandwidth control. For the latter, we introduce a tree-coupled max-min bandwidth-sharing model and show that tree duplication approximates an explicit fractional allocation with a provable accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Finally, we extend the fractional-packing framework to additional collective operations and multiple concurrent collective groups.
item.dc:creator: Namir Ballan, Reuven Cohen

item.title: Sample-Size Extrapolation in Simulation-Based Inference via Statistical Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2610.16820v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In simulation-based inference (SBI), neural posterior estimators trained on a bounded range of sample sizes can become inaccurate on larger datasets because their parameterizations do not specify how posterior location, uncertainty and shape must change as observations accumulate. We propose center-estimated NPE (CE-NPE), which combines a statistical center with an explicit contraction rate and learns a local center correction and residual densities in posterior-scale coordinates. The center is a statistical estimate, such as a closed-form statistic or a simulator-based moment match, which does not require an evaluable likelihood. Our analysis explains how contraction amplifies center error and decomposes Gaussian posterior error into shape, mean and covariance contributions. On six regular benchmarks, CE-NPE gives the best reference-posterior agreement of all tested amortized estimators at every out-of-range size, up to five times the largest training size, without retraining; it also fits better within the training range on most of them. Matched controls and nonregular examples characterize the scope of these gains and identify the conditions on which they depend: an appropriate contraction rate, an accurate center, and a stable residual representation.
item.dc:creator: Shiyi Sun, Lei Fang, Geoff K Nicholls

item.title: MODAIC: Coordinated Asynchrony for Decentralized Multimodal Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.16987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.
item.dc:creator: Yanhang Shi, Xiaoyu Wang, Houwei Cao, Jian Li, Yong Liu

item.title: Towards Resilience: Slice-Driven Orchestration of Mobile IoMT in 6G-Edge-Continuum
item.description: arXiv:2610.17296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Emerging healthcare services, such as real-time diagnostics, remote health monitoring and computer-assisted surgery, require stringent Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees while operating under limited and heterogeneous edge resources. Existing Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) orchestration methods primarily focus on communication metrics such as latency and bandwidth, while overlooking edge resource constraints and dynamic adaptation to workload and user mobility. This paper presents a novel resource-slicing-based adaptive orchestration framework that integrates 5G network slicing (NS), resource-aware orchestration, and mobility-aware task offloading into a single adaptive system. IoMT services are assigned to distinct 5G network slices while jointly considering CPU capacity, memory availability and amount of storage, enabling more efficient service placement and execution. In addition, the system supports user mobility and dynamic task offloading to maintain service continuity under changing network conditions. SimPy-based simulation demonstrates that the proposed method enhances service deployment efficiency, reduces request blocking, and improves user acceptance while maintaining reliable performance across diverse IoMT scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Zeeshan, Hafiz Faheem Shahid, Erkki Harjula

item.title: Beyond Model Scaling: Rethinking Sequence Construction for Transformer-based Network Intrusion Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.17725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformer-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) have shown strong potential for detecting multi-stage cyberattacks, yet most methods construct input sequences using fixed temporalization schemes rather than treating sequence construction as a systems design decision. In flow-based intrusion detection, timestamp-based windowing often fragments related attack activities while merging unrelated communications, reducing the behavioral context available to transformers. We present a unified pipeline abstraction that decomposes transformer-based NIDS into four design dimensions (traffic representation, temporalization, transformer backbone, and prediction aggregation) and propose session-coherent temporalization, which constructs sequences from communication sessions instead of fixed time windows. Experiments on three complementary intrusion detection datasets show that temporalization is the dominant factor governing transformer performance: session-coherent temporalization more than doubles Macro-F1 over timestamp-based windowing, enabling lightweight transformers to achieve up to 0.95 Macro-F1 at substantially higher inference throughput than pretrained models. We further vary the transformer size from 0.65M to 3.38M parameters and find that larger transformer models provide no measurable accuracy improvement despite substantially higher computational cost, while zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation shows only modest gains under domain shift. These results indicate that preserving communication-session semantics, rather than scaling transformer capacity, is the key to accurate and efficient transformer-based intrusion detection.
item.dc:creator: Zeeshan Zulkifl Shah, Muhammad Ikram, Dali Kaafar, Yipeng Zhou

item.title: FlowWise: Stateful Fast-Slow Model Serving for Streaming Traffic Intelligence
item.description: arXiv:2402.03694v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Network traffic analysis in cloud and internet service provider (ISP) networks increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) models, as encryption and service consolidation make rule-based classification unreliable. At high flow-arrival rates, however, new flows can arrive faster than end-to-end analysis pipelines can process. Unlike typical cloud inference workloads, packets from the same flow arrive over time and require per-flow state. This streaming, stateful setting limits naive scale-out with stateless workers. This paper presents FlowWise, a serving system for streaming, stateful flow intelligence on commodity CPU/GPU servers that jointly selects (i) how many packets to collect and (ii) which model(s) to apply for each flow to balance latency, service rate, and accuracy. Across three representative tasks, inference time across candidate models differs by 1.8x-141.3x, while packet waiting time can exceed feature computation and inference by 6-8 orders of magnitude at the tail. FlowWise exploits these gaps with an uncertainty-driven fast-slow cascade: it issues early predictions from a one-packet model and escalates only uncertain flows to slower models that wait for additional packets and use richer features. A queue-centric runtime maintains per-flow state, performs asynchronous feature joining, and uses brokered, flow-ID-keyed streams to distribute workload across heterogeneous workers. FlowWise serves 76.3% of flows within 16 ms, improving median end-to-end serving latency by 40.5x while increasing service rate and maintaining similar accuracy to always running the slow model. With thousands of packet-header features per flow, our scale-up benchmark sustains over 48.5k new flows per second on a single 16-core commodity CPU server, comparable to reported flow-arrival rates in city-backbone traces. FlowWise is open sourced at https://github.com/noise-lab/FlowWise.
item.dc:creator: Shinan Liu, Ted Shaowang, Gerry Wan, Jeewon Chae, Jonatas Marques, Sanjay Krishnan, Nick Feamster

item.title: Hybrid Wi-Fi/PDR Indoor Localization with Fingerprint Matching
item.description: arXiv:2505.08258v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Indoor position technology has become one of the research highlights in the Internet of Things (IoT), but there is still a lack of universal, low-cost, and high-precision solutions. This paper conducts research on indoor position technology based on location fingerprints and proposes a practical hybrid indoor positioning system. In this experiment, the location fingerprint database is established by using RSS signal in the offline stage, the location algorithm is improved and innovated in the online stage. The weighted k-nearest neighbor algorithm is used for location fingerprint matching and pedestrian dead reckoning technology is used for trajectory tracking. This paper designs and implements an indoor position system that performs the functions of data collection, positioning, and position tracking. Through the test, it is found that it can meet the requirements of indoor positioning.
item.dc:creator: Chunyi Zhang, Zongwei Li, Xiaoqi Li

item.title: Friend or Foe? Identifying Anomalous Peers in Moneros P2P Network
item.description: arXiv:2509.10214v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Monero, the leading privacy-focused cryptocurrency, relies on a peer-to-peer (P2P) network to propagate transactions and blocks. Growing evidence suggests that non-standard nodes exist in the network, posing as honest nodes but are perhaps intended for monitoring the network and spying on other nodes. However, our understanding of the detection and analysis of anomalous peer behavior remains limited. This paper presents a first comprehensive study of anomalous behavior in Monero's P2P network. To this end, we collected and analyzed over 240 hours of network traffic captured from five distinct vantage points worldwide. We further present a formal framework which allows us to analytically define and classify anomalous patterns in P2P cryptocurrency networks. Our detection methodology, implemented as an offline analysis, provides a foundation for real-time monitoring systems. Our analysis reveals the presence of non-standard peers in the network where approximately 14.74% (13.19%) of (reachable) peers in the network exhibit non-standard behavior. These peers exhibit distinct behavioral patterns that might suggest multiple concurrent attacks, pointing to substantial shortcomings in Monero's privacy guarantees and network decentralization. To support reproducibility and enable network operators to protect themselves, we release our examination pipeline to identify and block suspicious peers based on newly captured network traffic.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 8th Conference on Advances in Financial Technologies (AFT 2026)
item.dc:creator: Yannik Kopyciok, Stefan Schmid, Friedhelm Victor

item.title: Transport Programs: Specifying The Missing Layer Between Protocols and Stacks
item.description: arXiv:2509.21550v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Running code has long served two roles in transport protocol design: a medium for protocol development and a precise behavioral specification. Modern stacks increasingly struggle to serve either role because protocol logic is interwoven with platform-specific machinery for high performance. Changing or comparing protocol behavior therefore requires deep stack expertise, hindering protocol evolution and obscuring interoperability problems. We propose transport programs, a specification layer between natural-language protocol standards and stack implementations. Written in MTP, a stack-independent language, these programs state protocol decisions precisely while leaving execution machinery to each stack. MTP provides an explicit interface between protocol and stack experts: transport programs can run on MTP-compatible stacks, describe existing fixed-function implementations for behavioral comparison, and structure tasks for AI agents. We demonstrate MTP's benefits with three MTP-compatible stacks, two software and an FPGA prototype, on which we run programs for TCP, Homa, lightweight QUIC, and RoCEv2, comparing MTP descriptions of two TCP stacks to reveal interoperability issues, and creating an MTP-structured agentic pipeline that derives from RFCs a TCP MTP program that interoperates with NS3's TCP.

item.title: PACC: Protocol-Aware Cross-Layer Compression for Compact Network Traffic Representation
item.description: arXiv:2602.08331v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Network traffic classification underpins network security and management but faces growing challenges from pervasive encryption and evolving protocols. Existing representations involve clear trade-offs: hand-crafted flow statistics are efficient but lossy, raw-bit encodings can be accurate but costly, and pre-trained embeddings support transfer but often flatten the protocol stack and entangle cross-layer signals. We observe substantial redundancy both across and within network layers, which existing paradigms do not explicitly address, wasting capacity and encouraging shortcut learning that degrades generalization. To address this, we propose PACC, a redundancy-aware cross-layer representation framework. PACC models protocol layers as multiview inputs and learns faithful, compact projections factorized into shared (cross-layer) and private (layer-specific) components. It incorporates an information-preserving sparse segment representation to reduce structural repetition and supervised intra-layer filtering to suppress task-irrelevant semantic redundancy. A behavior-guided shared/private decomposition aligns cross-layer consensus while retaining layer-specific information, supported by information-theoretic analysis. Across encrypted application classification, IoT device identification, benign/malicious traffic classification, and Tor traffic detection, PACC achieves the best overall performance. On encrypted traffic, it achieves an F1 score of 0.9685, substantially outperforming existing baselines while using approximately 15x fewer computes and less GPU memory than the latest pre-trained traffic model.

item.title: Scheduling Parallel Optical Circuit Switches for AI Training
item.description: arXiv:2603.07373v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid growth of AI training has dramatically increased datacenter traffic demand and energy consumption, which has motivated renewed interest in optical circuit switches (OCSes) as a high-bandwidth, energy-efficient alternative for AI fabrics. Deploying multiple parallel OCSes is a leading alternative. However, efficiently scheduling time-varying traffic matrices across parallel optical switches with non-negligible reconfiguration delays remains an open challenge. We consider the problem of scheduling a single AI traffic demand matrix $D$ over $s$ parallel OCSes while minimizing the makespan under reconfiguration delay $\delta$. Our algorithm Spectra relies on a three-step approach: Decompose $D$ into a minimal set of weighted permutations; Schedule these permutations across parallel switches using load-aware assignment; then Equalize the imbalanced loads on the switches via controlled permutation splitting. Evaluated on realistic AI training workloads (GPT model and Qwen MoE expert routing) as well as standard benchmarks, Spectra vastly outperforms a baseline based on state-of-the-art algorithms, reducing schedule makespan by an average factor of $1.4\times$ on GPT AI workloads, $2.7\times$ on MoE AI workloads, and $2.4\times$ on standard benchmarks. Further, the makespans achieved by Spectra consistently approach newly derived lower bounds.

item.title: AEGIS: Risk-Budgeted Online Scheduling for Resilient Continuous Edge Inference
item.description: arXiv:2605.02179v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous edge inference requires sustained wireless and computing support across successive service instances. Under recurring channel degradation, transient edge overload, and multi-user contention, isolated deadline misses may accumulate into persistent service degradation. Existing schedulers mainly optimize instantaneous latency or per-timeslot utility and provide limited control over such cross-time effects. To address this issue, we propose AEGIS (Adaptive Exposure-Governed Inference Scheduling), a risk-budgeted online framework for service-level operational resilience. AEGIS regulates predicted deadline-risk exposure through dynamically replenished per-user risk budgets and establishes an explicit finite-horizon bound on cumulative admitted-risk exposure. One-step state estimation supports anticipatory delay and risk assessment, while the centralized bandwidth-computing allocation is transformed into an exact-potential formulation and solved through asynchronous coordinate updates. Simulation results under varying system scales and stress conditions show that adaptive replenishment improves service continuity and recovery relative to fixed replenishment, while risk budgeting reduces predicted-risk exposure compared with more aggressive scheduling alternatives.
