item.title: Energy Consumption in Next Generation Radio Access Networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.11899v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Historically, in macro-cell-based networks, the radio access network (RAN) portion accounts for the largest share of energy consumption in mobile networks. With greater densification, the transition to small cells and increased virtualization of the radio processing functions, the relative energy use of the different network segments is changing. At the same time, open radio access networks (O-RAN) have emerged as a promising approach to support this evolution through open interfaces that enable a multi-vendor environment, support for hierarchical intelligent controls, and simplified, cost-effective radio units that facilitate large-scale deployments. This paper examines the impact of these changes on energy consumption in next-generation RAN architectures through transaction-based energy models. Transaction-based network energy models were developed in 2009 to understand the evolution of energy use in networks. Here we update these models with today's hardware and apply recently developed models for emerging architectures, considering current access point densification trends. Results indicate that efficiency improvements have followed predicted trends, which were largely based on semiconductor Moore's Law-related evolution. Emerging RAN architectures show improved energy per bit, although the processing energy becomes the largest contributor. Densification increases total energy consumption, but the relative contributions of processing and transport energy depend strongly on the location of the baseband processing.

item.title: TraceCodec: A Compiler-Backed Neural Codec for Network Traffic Traces
item.description: arXiv:2605.29941v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Critical networking workflows require high-fidelity packet captures (PCAPs) for testing, security analysis, and protocol validation, not just statistical flow-level summaries. Recent packet generators have demonstrated protocol-constrained PCAP synthesis, but many operate on raw or near-raw packet representations. These representations can entangle learned behavioral choices with deterministic protocol rules and make packet correctness depend on post-hoc repair. We identify the decode interface as a key bottleneck and present TraceCodec, a compiler-backed neural codec for stateful multi-flow traces. TraceCodec lifts each parsed packet into a timed packet action with explicit flow slots and transport cues, learns a continuous per-packet latent, and uses a state-aware deterministic compiler to decode actions to PCAPs while managing endpoint assignment, TCP sequence and acknowledgment state, declared compatibility constraints, and packet rendering. On CICIDS2017 Monday, TraceCodec matches packet count, protocol composition, and flow population to within 0.03%; raw-field baselines produce substantially larger flow-count and TCP-event errors under the same non-repair policy. In a matched flow-matching continuation setup, TraceCodec yields complete decoded suffixes in 100% of CICIDS2017 cases and 98.44% of MAWI cases, versus at most 10.94% for raw-field latent controls. Structural diagnostics further show that TraceCodec preserves TCP transitions and multi-flow interleaving. Together, these results support TraceCodec as a generator-facing latent interface with a deterministic path back to usable packet traces.

item.title: When Unlearning Fails: Reliable Data Deletion under Post-Training in Agent Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.28829v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Embedded AI agents on edge devices can learn as a federation and keep improving after deployment. Each agent collects new trajectories with the current policy, and the edge server aggregates them in later rounds. In such self-improving agent networks, deleting data is harder than a one-time model repair. The data to be deleted may have already shaped later retained trajectories, so retraining or model-side unlearning leaves an influence echo that returns as the network keeps learning. We propose Muting Unlearned Trajectories' Echoes (MUTE) for reliable deletion over edge networks. MUTE traces the echo from a lightweight ledger at the edge server, without moving raw trajectories off the devices. It erases the current residue with a forget-retain update, contains high-influence retained trajectories, and audits later behavior to schedule further erasure under the uplink budget and the response deadline. On LIBERO, MUTE keeps the regenerated share of forgotten behavior at or below 0.401 for every request type, against at least 0.466 for five recent methods.
item.dc:creator: Zihao Ding, Jun Huang, Liang Dong

item.title: Teleoperated Driving: a New Challenge for 3D Object Detection in Compressed Point Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2506.11804v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In recent years, the development of interconnected devices has expanded in many fields, from infotainment to education and industrial applications. This trend has been accelerated by the increased number of low-cost sensors and accessibility to powerful hardware and software. One area that significantly benefits from these advancements is Teleoperated Driving. In this scenario, a remote controller (human or software) safely drives a vehicle using sensor data generated onboard the vehicle, and exchanged via Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this work, we tackle the problem of detecting the presence of cars, pedestrians, and cyclists from point cloud data generated by LiDAR sensors to enable safe Teleoperated Driving operations. Specifically, we use the SELMA dataset, a multimodal, open-source, synthetic dataset for autonomous driving, that we expanded by including the ground-truth bounding boxes of 3D objects to support object detection. We analyze the performance of state-of-the-art compression algorithms and object detectors under several metrics, including compression efficiency, (de)compression and inference time, and detection accuracy. Finally, we measure the impact of compression and detection on a simulated V2X network in terms of data rate and latency with respect to the 3GPP requirements of Teleoperated Driving applications. Our results show that G-PCC outperforms its competitors in terms of both compression efficiency and accuracy, and consumes fewer channel resources for data transmissions. On the contrary, the two most conservative quantization modes of Draco, combined with SECOND or PointPillars for object detection, offer superior speed in both compression and decompression with comparable accuracy. Finally, we show that the choice of the detector depends on the class of objects to detect, specifically pedestrians or cyclists.

item.title: Detecting Data Exfiltration through I2P Anonymity Networks: A Two-Phase Machine Learning Approach
item.description: arXiv:2605.20546v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Invisible Internet Project (I2P) provides strong anonymity through garlic routing and distributed network architecture, making it attractive for legitimate privacy needs. Nevertheless, the same properties can be exploited by malicious actors to steal sensitive information from corporate networks without detection. Current network security measures often fail to detect I2P traffic, and existing literature has focused primarily on protocol-level traffic identification without addressing behavioral threat assessment. This paper proposes a two-stage machine-learning model for I2P traffic analysis using the SafeSurf Darknet 2025 dataset comprising 184,548 network flows. Phase 1 achieved 99.96% accuracy in distinguishing I2P traffic from normal network traffic using a Random Forest classifier, with only 2 false positives among 32,318 normal flows. Phase 2 performed behavioral analysis on traffic identified as I2P, classifying it as either exfiltration or legitimate activity, achieving 91.11% accuracy using XGBoost. The system demonstrates that tree-based ensemble methods substantially outperform deep neural networks and support vector machines for this task. Feature importance analysis indicates that the most discriminative features are packet timing and flow duration. These findings establish that accurate I2P traffic detection and threat prioritization are achievable in operational network environments, enabling security teams to focus resources on high-risk events rather than monitoring all encrypted traffic.

item.title: Deploying RDMA for Distributed Inference and Training At Scale
item.description: arXiv:2610.12815v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: RDMA can reduce communication overhead in distributed machine learning systems, but realizing these benefits in production requires more than replacing TCP. Variable-size messages, concurrent connections, bursty incasts, and service failures introduce challenges that hardware offload alone cannot address. This paper reports our experience deploying ByteExpress, a software communication layer over hardware RDMA, in ByteDance's parameter-server-based inference and training systems. We present three lessons from the deployment: efficient RDMA requires buffer management across application and transport layers; scalable communication requires coordinated management of connections, receive capacity, and outstanding data; and service availability requires recovery above the transport layer. ByteExpress combines an RDMA-aware allocator, zero-copy transfers, QP multiplexing, receive-credit flow control, a software send window, and RPC-assisted recovery. In production inference, ByteExpress reduces mean and P99 model parameter fetch latency by 35.7% and 43.7%, respectively, and total CPU usage by 10.69% compared with kernel TCP. In training, ByteExpress reduces P99 model parameter push latency by up to 74.0% compared with TCP, with no PFC pauses observed at runtime.
